#21933. Orbis 2: A Hierarchical World Model for Driving

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (211 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Orbis 2: A Hierarchical World Model for Driving

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (211 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2607.15898v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Current world models operate at a single level of abstraction, with most prioritizing perceptual fidelity while lacking the spatial reasoning and semantic understanding required for real-world downstream tasks. We present a hierarchical driving world model that factorizes future prediction across two levels operating at distinct temporal and abstraction scales: a high-level predictor that forecasts coarse scene structure over extended temporal horizons, and a low-level generator that produces detailed predictions conditioned on the high-level output. This decomposition yields high perceptual fidelity while also capturing strong spatial and semantic representations. We further show that pretraining with a diffusion forcing objective yields substantially richer internal representations than the standard teacher forcing objective, while teacher forcing -- predicting only the next frame from clean context -- produces more stable autoregressive rollouts. We therefore introduce a generic two-stage training paradigm that pretrains the model with diffusion forcing and fine-tunes with teacher forcing, combining the representational benefits of the former with the rollout stability of the latter. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results across the standard suite of driving world model evaluations on established benchmarks, including long-horizon generation fidelity, steering responsiveness evaluated on counterfactual scenarios, and internal representation quality. Project page with code, demo, checkpoints and qualitative results: https://lmb-freiburg.github.io/orbis2.github.io/.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (139 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2601.20263v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) is a quantum computational model that leverages linear optics to solve sampling problems believed to be classically intractable. Recent experimental breakthroughs have demonstrated quantum advantage using GBS, motivating its application to real-world combinatorial optimization problems. In this work, we reformulate the graph coloring problem as an integer programming problem using the independent set formulation. This enables the use of GBS to identify cliques in the complement graph, which correspond to independent sets in the original graph. Our method is benchmarked against classical heuristics and exact algorithms on two sets of instances: Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random graphs and graphs derived from a smart-charging use case. The results demonstrate that GBS can provide competitive solutions, highlighting its potential as a quantum-enhanced heuristic for graph-based optimization.

#21928. Grounding Driving VLA via Inverse Kinematics

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (188 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Grounding Driving VLA via Inverse Kinematics

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (188 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2605.21061v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Counterfactual obstacle insertion exposes blind planning in representative Driving VLAs: their trajectories remain largely unchanged despite a vehicle appearing directly ahead. An empirically calibrated bias-variance analysis identifies how ego-predictable training examples admit a shortcut through ego status and commands. We address this failure with an inverse-kinematics-inspired architecture that anchors trajectory decoding on current and predicted future visual states. First, a next visual state prediction objective that requires the LLM to predict the future visual scene provides dense visual supervision and suppresses shortcut paths. Second, a separate Inverse Kinematics Network (a cross-attention-based conditional diffusion model) that takes only the current and future visual states as input is designed to suppress reliance on ego status and textual shortcuts during trajectory decoding. Our 0.5B model achieves state-of-the-art trajectory planning performance on NAVSIM-v1, NAVSIM-v2, and nuScenes using cameras alone, without LiDAR or a BEV encoder. Against the matched OpenDriveVLA* baseline, it improves NAVSIM PDMS and EPDMS by 19.0 and 20.4 points, respectively. Controlled ablations and intervention analyses support improved use of visual features, with future-state prediction sharpening hazard-specific responses.

#21925. Realisation of a Protected Cat-Qutrit Manifold via Engineered Quantum Tunnelling

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (215 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Realisation of a Protected Cat-Qutrit Manifold via Engineered Quantum Tunnelling

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (215 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2601.17675v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Engineering quantum tunnelling in phase space has emerged as a viable method for creating a protected logical qubit manifold with biased-noise properties. A promising approach is to combine a Kerr nonlinearity with a multi-photon drive, resulting in a system known as a Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO). In this work, we implement a three-photon KPO and explore its potential as a protected bosonic qutrit. We confirm quantum coherence by demonstrating three-photon Rabi oscillations and performing direct Wigner function measurements that reveal the formation of three-component cat-like states. Crucially, we observe a breathing-like dynamic in phase space, a characteristic feature of driven quantum systems. This dynamic arises from macroscopic temporal interference between the cat-qutrit manifold and the excited states. The frequency of resulting oscillations in the mean photon number provides a direct, time-domain measurement of the energy gap separating the qutrit from the excited states, thereby establishing an experimental hallmark of qutrit manifold protection. Furthermore, we identify a parasitic higher-order pump term as the primary mechanism constraining the mean photon number, highlighting its mitigation as a requisite for maximising protection. Our findings elucidate the basic quantum properties of the three-photon KPO and establish the first step towards its use as an alternative qutrit platform.

#21919. DeformMaster: An Interactive Physics-Neural World Model for Deformable Objects from Videos

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (200 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

DeformMaster: An Interactive Physics-Neural World Model for Deformable Objects from Videos

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (200 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2605.09586v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: World models for deformable objects should recover not only geometry and appearance, but also underlying physical dynamics, interaction grounding, and material behavior. Learning such a model from real videos is challenging because deformable linear, planar, and volumetric objects evolve under high-dimensional deformation, noisy interactions, and complex material response. The model must infer a physical state from visual observations, roll it forward under upcoming interactions, and render the resulting dynamics with high visual fidelity. We therefore present DeformMaster, a video-derived interactive physics-neural world model that turns real interaction videos into an online interactive model of deformable objects within a unified dynamics-and-appearance framework. DeformMaster preserves structured physical rollout while using a neural residual to compensate for unmodeled effects, grounds sparse hand motion as distributed compliant actuators for hand-continuum interaction, represents material response with spatially varying constitutive experts, and drives high-fidelity 4D appearance from the predicted physical evolution. Experiments on real-world deformable-object sequences demonstrate DeformMaster's ability to roll out future dynamics and render dynamic appearance, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines while supporting novel action rollout, material-parameter variation, and dynamic novel-view synthesis. Code and video demos are available at the project page: https://can-lee.github.io/deformmaster-web/.

#21917. Breaking: Group Fourier filtering of quantum resources in quantum phase space

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (209 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Group Fourier filtering of quantum resources in quantum phase space

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (209 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2601.14225v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recently, it has been shown that group Fourier analysis of quantum states, i.e., decomposing them into the irreducible representations (irreps) of a symmetry group, enables fresh ways to characterize their resourcefulness. Given that quantum phase spaces (QPSs) provide an alternative description of quantum systems, and thus of the group's representation, one may wonder how such harmonic analysis changes. In this work we show that for general compact Lie-group quantum resource theories (QRTs), the entire family of Stratonovich-Weyl quantum phase-space representations, characterized by the Cahill--Glauber parameter $s$, has a clear resource-theoretic and signal-processing meaning. Specifically, changing $s$ implements a continuously tunable group Fourier filter. In the examples of spin coherence, multipartite entanglement, and fermionic Gaussianity, this gives a low-pass representation at $s=-1$, an unfiltered spectrum at $s=0$, and a high-pass representation at $s=1$. Moreover, we show that the norms of the QRT's free-state Fourier components completely determine this family of phase-space representations. Finally, we uncover an $s$-duality relating the nontrivial phase-space spectra of free states to the ensemble-averaged spectra of typical (Haar-random) states through a shift in $s$. Overall, our results provide a new interpretation of QPSs and establish them as a signal-processing framework for characterizing, filtering, and visualizing quantum resources.

Industry News: Integrated Generation and Purification of Entangled Coherent States for Non-Gaussian Teleportation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (233 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2512.10225v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Entangled coherent states (ECS) provide a powerful non-Gaussian resource for continuous-variable (CV) quantum communication, but their generation in scalable architectures remains challenging. We propose an integrated photonic scheme that creates high-fidelity quasi-entangled coherent states (quasi-ECS) from a two-mode squeezed vacuum state (TMSVS) via photon subtraction in a symmetric waveguide trimer. The resulting non-Gaussian entanglement is further enhanced by single-photon catalysis, which purifies the distributed state after transmission through lossy channels. The improvement in conditional teleportation fidelity is accompanied by a reduced heralding probability. Using these purified quasi-ECS resources, we analyze a photon-number-based teleportation protocol and demonstrate high-fidelity transfer of both coherent states and Schrodinger cat states. For the logical cat qubit, we use an orthogonal even/odd-cat basis, measurement-dependent phase corrections, and the success-probability-weighted fidelity over six logical input states. For completeness and benchmarking, we also study the Braunstein-Kimble (BK) teleportation protocol using Gaussian TMSVSs. In particular, the teleportation fidelity for cat states exceeds the benchmark value of 2/3 over a broad range of realistic channel and squeezing parameters. By contrast, the underlying TMSVS performs poorly within the photon-number-based protocol, whereas in the BK protocol it exceeds this benchmark only in a restricted regime of high squeezing and high transmissivity. Our results show that integrated photon subtraction and catalysis enable practical, chip-compatible generation of non-Gaussian entanglement suitable for advanced quantum teleportation and CV quantum networks.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Improved parameter initialization for the (local) unitary cluster Jastrow ansatz

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (247 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2511.22476v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The unitary cluster Jastrow (UCJ) ansatz and its variant known as local UCJ (LUCJ) are promising choices for variational quantum algorithms for chemistry due to their combination of physical motivation and hardware efficiency. The parameters of these ansatzes can be initialized from the output of a coupled cluster, singles and doubles (CCSD) calculation performed on a classical computer. However, truncating the number of repetitions of the ansatz, as well as discarding interactions to accommodate the connectivity constraints of near-term quantum processors, degrade the approximation to CCSD and the resulting energy accuracy. In this work, we propose two methods to improve the parameter initialization. The first method, which is applicable to both expectation value- and sample-based algorithms, uses compressed double factorization of the CCSD amplitudes to improve or recover the CCSD approximation. The second method, which is applicable to sample-based algorithms, uses approximate tensor network simulation to improve the quality of samples produced by the ansatz circuit. Both methods perform classical preprocessing to construct the initial circuit parameters and can be followed by parameter optimization using quantum measurements, although we do not perform such optimization in this work. We validate our methods using exact state vector simulation on systems of up to 52 qubits, as well as experiments on superconducting quantum processors using up to 65 qubits. Our results indicate that our methods can significantly improve the output of both expectation value- and sample-based quantum algorithms.

#21905. AAC: Admissible-by-Architecture Differentiable Landmark Compression for ALT

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (237 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

AAC: Admissible-by-Architecture Differentiable Landmark Compression for ALT

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (237 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2604.20744v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce the Architecturally Admissible Compressor (AAC), which adapts landmark-based A* heuristics to query demand under a fixed label-memory budget. AAC provides two continuous relaxations of ALT (A*, Landmarks, and Triangle inequality) selection. With exact landmark distances, every parameter value defines a lower bound on shortest-path distance. Both relaxations deploy ALT using only the selected labels. The row-stochastic relaxation takes convex combinations of landmark distances. We characterize the maximal admissibility-preserving linear classes and prove that the relaxed and discrete optima coincide. The fractional relaxation mixes subset heuristics and supports continuous greedy (AAC-CG) with exact gradients and an entropy-regularized oracle for differentiable selection. For expected heuristic value, we prove an approximation guarantee with finite-step, oracle-error, and finite-sample terms. The limiting $1-1/e$ factor is optimal for arbitrary supplied pools and query distributions unless P${=}$NP. At matched label memory, AAC-CG reduces A* expansions by $1.9$-$22.7$% relative to farthest-point ALT (FPS-ALT) in all $19$ tested combinations of graph and memory budget across six road networks and two synthetic graphs. Each combination uses one $500$-query test split; all methods share distance tables when distances are symmetric. Canonical greedy also expands fewer nodes than FPS-ALT in all $19$ graph-budget pairs. AAC-CG achieves $99.6$% of canonical greedy's mean heuristic value on test queries, averaged over these pairs. AAC makes admissibility independent of training success, while its analysis and experiments distinguish selection quality from search efficiency.

Tasks arrive online over a finite horizon and must be completed within specified deadlines, while agents operate from distributed hubs with limited sensing and communication. We model incomplete information through hub-based sensing regions that determine task visibility and a communication graph that governs inter-hub information exchange. Using this framework, we propose Iterative Best Response (IBR), a decentralized policy in which each agent selects the task that maximizes its marginal contribution to the locally observed welfare. We compare IBR against three baselines: Earliest Due Date first (EDD), Hungarian algorithm, and Stochastic Conflict-Based Allocation (SCoBA), on a city-scale package-delivery domain with up to 100 drones and varying task arrival scenarios. Under full and sparse communication, IBR achieves competitive task-completion performance with lower computation time.

#21893. Tech Report: Harnessing Intrinsic Noise for Quantum Simulation of Open Quantum Systems

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (168 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Harnessing Intrinsic Noise for Quantum Simulation of Open Quantum Systems

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (168 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2510.21075v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulating open quantum systems on quantum computers is challenging because dissipative dynamics are nonunitary, whereas gate-based quantum algorithms are typically built from unitary operations. Conventional approaches can overcome this mismatch by embedding nonunitary processes into enlarged unitary circuits, often with ancillary-qubit and gate overhead. In this work, we propose an alternative perspective in which we selectively preserve the physical noise to emulate nonunitary channels. More specifically, we present a partial encoding algorithm that iteratively leverages intrinsic noise to mimic the dynamics of a target open-system. We benchmark the convergence of this algorithm against the dissipative exciton transport Hamiltonian and retrieve their dynamics. By utilizing intrinsic hardware noise to emulate the target nonunitary dynamics, this approach avoids the dual overhead of error-correcting that noise and using ancillary qubits to re-introduce nonunitarity. This significantly reduces both qubit requirements and physical fidelity thresholds, paving the way for more efficient techniques to simulate open quantum systems on quantum computers.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2510.20096v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A core problem in communications is the optimal discrimination of binary-phase-shift-keyed (BPSK) signals. A longstanding goal has been to reach the fundamental quantum limit, known as the Helstrom bound, for BPSK signals encoded in coherent states. However, due to technical constraints, proposals for reaching the bound remain impractical. In this letter we take an alternative approach: using only Gaussian optics - displaced squeezed states and homodyne detection - we achieve discrimination of BPSK signals with error rates below what can be achieved using coherent states and any quantum measurement.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2603.06531v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffuse direct time-of-flight LiDARs report per-pixel depth histograms formed by aggregating photon returns over a wide instantaneous field of view, violating the single-ray assumption behind standard LiDAR-RGB calibration. We present a simple spatial calibration procedure that estimates, for each diffuse LiDAR pixel, its footprint (effective support region) and relative spatial sensitivity in a co-located RGB image plane. Using a scanned retroreflective patch with background subtraction, we recover per-pixel response maps that provide an explicit LiDAR-to-RGB correspondence for cross-modal alignment and fusion. We demonstrate the method on the ams OSRAM TMF8828.

#21855. Long-Term Multi-Session 3D Reconstruction Under Substantial Appearance Change

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (234 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Long-Term Multi-Session 3D Reconstruction Under Substantial Appearance Change

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (234 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2602.20584v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-term environmental monitoring requires the ability to reconstruct and align 3D models across repeated site visits separated by months or years to enable the detection of structural change and the assessment of ecosystem health. However, existing Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines are generally designed for imagery captured within a limited time window and consequently fail in long-term monitoring scenarios such as repeated coral reef surveys with substantial visual and structural change. In this paper, we show that the primary limitation of current approaches lies in their inability to maintain visual correspondences under substantial temporal appearance change. We address this limitation by enforcing cross-session correspondences within a joint SfM reconstruction. Our approach combines handcrafted and learned visual features to establish correspondences across large temporal gaps, enabling the reconstruction of a single coherent 3D model from imagery captured years apart, where standard SfM fails to connect sessions. To ensure scalability and further improve alignment robustness on large datasets, we restrict expensive learned feature matching to a small set of likely cross-session image pairs identified via visual place recognition, which reduces computational cost while improving the reliability of cross-session correspondence establishment. We evaluate our method on long-term underwater datasets exhibiting significant real-world change, and demonstrate consistent joint reconstruction across sessions in cases where existing methods fail to connect the sessions or align them only coarsely.

#21845. Breaking: Sparse Video Generation Propels Real-World Beyond-the-View Vision-Language Navigation

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (231 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Sparse Video Generation Propels Real-World Beyond-the-View Vision-Language Navigation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (231 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2602.05827v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Why must vision-language navigation be bound to detailed and verbose language instructions? While such details ease decision-making, they fundamentally contradict the goal for navigation in the real-world. Ideally, agents should possess the autonomy to navigate in unknown environments guided solely by simple and high-level intents. Realizing this ambition introduces a formidable challenge: Beyond-the-View Navigation (BVN), where agents must locate distant, unseen targets without dense and step-by-step guidance. Existing large language model (LLM)-based methods, though adept at following dense instructions, often suffer from short-sighted behaviors due to their reliance on short-horimzon supervision. Simply extending the supervision horizon, however, destabilizes LLM training. In this work, we identify that video generation models inherently benefit from long-horizon supervision to align with language instructions, rendering them uniquely suitable for BVN tasks. Capitalizing on this insight, we propose introducing the video generation model into this field for the first time. Yet, the prohibitive latency for generating videos spanning tens of seconds makes real-world deployment impractical. To bridge this gap, we propose SparseVideoNav, achieving sub-second trajectory inference guided by a generated sparse future spanning a 20-second horizon. This yields a remarkable 27x speed-up compared to the unoptimized counterpart. Extensive real-world zero-shot experiments demonstrate that SparseVideoNav achieves 2.5x the success rate of state-of-the-art LLM baselines on BVN tasks and marks the first realization of such capability in challenging night scenes.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2506.13624v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a GPU-based solver for trajectory planning problems using branch model predictive control. Building on iterative LQR methods, we adopt a multiple-shooting formulation for the system dynamics and use an augmented Lagrangian method to handle general stage-wise constraints. This design enables straightforward warm-starting. The constraint-handling capability of our solver is validated on two challenging trajectory planning problems. In addition, we develop two tailored inner LQR solvers that exploit the tree-sparse structure. The solvers offer different levels of parallelism, making them appropriate for different tree sizes. The numerical results demonstrate that, compared to a high-performance CPU-based solver, our approach achieves superior performance on large-scale problems.

arXiv:2510.14289v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We revisit the Bohr-Sommerfeld atomic model to explore hydrogen-like ions of Uranium ($Z=92$), Oganesson ($Z=118$), and hypothetical superheavy elements beyond. Although superseded by the Dirac equation and modern quantum electrodynamics, the semiclassical approach offers a historically and pedagogically valuable perspective. Using the Sommerfeld fine structure formula and computer algebra methods, we demonstrate the appearance of self-intersecting orbits in super strong Coulomb fields, beginning with Oganesson and hypothetical elements up to $Z\le137$. These orbits can be classified by their `winding' numbers, providing a simple topological description of Coulomb field strength in this framework. Our results highlight a conceptual bridge between early quantum theory and modern superheavy element physics.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (129 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2508.16691v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present an operational reconstruction of the well-known two-to-one homomorphism between the groups $SU(2)$ and $SO(3)$, grounded in the physical description of quantum state preparation and evolution. Starting from the connection between vectors in three-dimensional physical space and quantum states of two-level systems, we investigate how reversible transformations-modeled as completely positive and trace-preserving maps-give rise to a correspondence between spatial rotations and unitary operations. Our approach reveals how this group-theoretic structure naturally emerges from physical constraints, particularly the preservation of purity and reversibility in quantum processes. Beyond its theoretical relevance, the construction offers a pedagogically accessible framework for introducing core ideas in quantum mechanics and symmetry groups, making the abstract correspondence between $SU(2)$ and $SO(3)$ tangible through experimentally meaningful procedures.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (149 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2501.16698v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Spatial intelligence, encompassing 3D perception and reasoning, is the essential next frontier of AI. Scaling current 3D vision-language models (VLMs) that rely on dense Transformers for spatial tasks incurs prohibitive computational costs. In this paper, we introduce 3D-MoE, a 3D VLM leveraging an efficient mixture-of-experts architecture with a modality- and spatial-context-aware probabilistic routing scheme, stably cultivated by a novel routing curriculum. To seamlessly extend 3D-MoE to embodied AI, we integrate a diffusion-based action head, Pose-DiT, transforming 3D-MoE into a 3D vision-language-action (VLA) model. By employing a rectified flow framework, Pose-DiT generates precise 6D pose actions in a single sampling step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that 3D-MoE achieves superior performance on diverse 3D vision-language benchmarks with drastically fewer activated parameters and yields higher success rates while enabling real-time inference for robot manipulation tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/yueen-ma/3D-MoE.

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: ESI: An Embodied Self-Improvement Flywheel for LLM-VLA Agents

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (245 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.18176v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Independently pretrained language models and vision-language-action (VLA) policies provide complementary building blocks for embodied agents, but connecting them does not automatically produce coordinated behavior. The VLA may generate actions that diverge from the LLM's intended subtask and, upon regaining control after a correction, undo the promising state restored by the LLM. We introduce ESI (Embodied Self-Improvement), an automated flywheel that uses environmental interaction to align reasoning and action. ESI treats the modular agent as the unit of post-training, repeatedly refining the prompts that guide the LLM, the shared skill interface that expresses its intent, and the VLA parameters that realize that intent, then redeploying these components together. Our key insight is that collaboration itself can supply supervision for improving this interface. The LLM's subtask decisions provide semantic supervision for what the policy should execute, while its effective corrections and subsequent student continuations provide action-level supervision for recovery and handoff. The student also learns from its own effective execution, allowing locally useful experience to contribute even when the overall episode fails. On ten selected RoboDojo tasks, ESI achieves a mean Score of 62.03 and a mean success rate of 49.41% using an LLM-VLA agent without generating task-specific control code. On both metrics, it outperforms the published reference results of all hybrid embodied agents, including the Agent+WAM system GO-3 Nano Preview (47.27 Score and 36.60% success), as well as all compared code-based methods.

Latest Update: Geometric encoding of turbulence for end-to-end quantum simulation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (168 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2508.05346v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulating multiscale turbulence in engineering remains challenging. Any quantum advantage for such simulations requires efficient initial-state preparation. Yet exact loading of an arbitrary classical snapshot requires exponential quantum resources. We introduce "turbuloscope", a physics-informed geometric method that generates statistically representative turbulent initial states in a gate-based register from a parameterized Pauli-spinor multiscale distribution. Scale invariance renders conditional rotations approximately affine in Gray-code space, enabling linear-depth, ancilla-free preparation. The generalized Madelung transform and Hopf fibration map the encoded Pauli spinor to fluid observables and vortex tubes. The qubit count scales logarithmically with the Reynolds number, yielding an exponential reduction in preparation overhead relative to full-grid classical spectral synthesis. We classically emulate a 30-qubit preparation circuit and generate a turbulent field over one billion grid points at a scale-inferred Reynolds number of 35,000, exhibiting Kolmogorov's five-thirds energy spectrum, tangled vortex tubes, and intermittency. This method provides scalable initial states for quantum simulation of turbulence and multiscale systems.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

A Generalizable Approach to Safety-Aware Robotic Behavior Planning with an Explicit Constraint Space

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (206 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.18026v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language and vision-language models have substantially advanced robotic behavior planning from natural-language instructions and visual observations. However, safe manipulation in tabletop environments remains challenging because the safety constraints required for a task depend on the surrounding scene and may not be explicitly specified in the instruction. We propose a safety-aware behavior planning framework based on an explicit Constraint Space that stores reusable textual safety rules. Rather than retrieving rules solely by semantic similarity, we formulate constraint selection as task- and environment-conditioned applicability learning. A lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model identifies the constraints applicable to the current context, which are then provided together with the original task and image to a multimodal behavior planner. To handle incorrect constraint selections and previously unseen hazards, we introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that evaluates generated primitive aims, reconstructs the complete applicable constraint set, and provides corrective planning feedback. Validated inspection feedback is further used for test-time adaptation of constraint applicability and parameter-efficient adaptation of the Safety Inspector through LoRA, while newly identified constraints are incorporated into the Constraint Space. The resulting framework integrates explicit safety knowledge representation,context-aware constraint selection, corrective safety inspection, and test-time knowledge adaptation for safety-aware robotic behavior planning.

In a recent development, arXiv:2507.15453v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding how decoherence-induced loss affects entanglement and nonlocal correlations in quantum memories is notable for quantum information science. Here we develop a quantitative description of photonic quantum states retrieved from electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) memories in a ground-state-decoherence-limited regime. Using the dark-state-polariton formalism, we derive the attenuation factor of the retrieved probe mode from the EIT dynamics. This attenuation depends on the coupling field and ground-state coherence decay and is not introduced as an independent phenomenological loss parameter. Within a specified quantum-limited pure-loss model, we use this attenuation to obtain the reduced photonic density operator. We show that, in the symmetric case, the complete retrieved state of an initially path-entangled single photon remains entangled for any nonzero storage efficiency, despite acquiring a vacuum component. In contrast, violation of the unconditional Clauser-Horne inequality under displaced on/off detection without post-selection requires an intrinsic efficiency above 89.7%. We further derive the retrieved N-qubit photonic density operator for multiple independently operating EIT memories. These results establish a quantitative connection between EIT memory dynamics, retrieved quantum states, and operational nonlocality benchmarks under explicit channel assumptions.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.17442v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How do action budgets shape vision-language navigation (VLN) exploration, and what expert supervision best teaches budget-aware search? We study budget-conditioned object search: finding as many distinct instances of a requested category as possible within a budget, with discovery defined geometrically by camera field of view and proximity. Distinct discoveries provide a denser evaluation signal than single-target success. We cast expert design as a choice of scene abstraction: a single budget-indexed Bellman recursion, applied to different abstractions of the full environment, yields experts that differ in what they know. An object-level Bellman expert is given every target location and reduces search to budgeted routing. A room-level Bellman expert retains observed room connectivity, doorway evidence, and cross-scene semantic priors but withholds the contents of unexplored rooms, so it must search for targets that its student also cannot see. We distill both experts into Uni-NaVid under matched training conditions and also evaluate greedy-frontier supervision on held-out HM3D scenes. Changing only the stated budget changes learned trajectories. Despite higher object-level expert return, room-level supervision achieves the highest mean collection among evaluated VLNs at every tested budget. At 2000 steps, it finds 72.7% of reachable targets, versus 68.5% under greedy-frontier supervision, 65.5% under object-level supervision, and 44.8% for the pretrained VLN. These results show that expert-return rankings need not predict supervision quality for VLN exploration, and motivate choosing an expert's abstraction with the student's information in mind rather than by expert return alone.

Quantum Advantage in Storage and Retrieval of Isometry Channels

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (249 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2507.10784v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Storage and retrieval refer to the task of encoding an unknown quantum channel $\Lambda$ into a quantum state, known as the program state, such that the channel can later be retrieved. There are two strategies for this task: classical and quantum strategies. The classical strategy uses multiple queries to $\Lambda$ to estimate $\Lambda$ and retrieves the channel based on the estimate represented in classical bits. The classical strategy turns out to offer the optimal performance for the storage and retrieval of unitary channels. In this work, we analyze the asymptotic performance of the classical and quantum strategies for the storage and retrieval of isometry channels. We show that the optimal fidelity for isometry estimation is given by $F = 1-{d(D-d)\over n} + O(n^{-4/3})$, where $d$ and $D$ denote the input and output dimensions of the isometry, and $n$ is the number of queries. This result indicates that, unlike in the case of unitary channels, the classical strategy is suboptimal for the storage and retrieval of isometry channels, which requires $n = \Theta(\epsilon^{-1})$ to achieve the diamond-norm error $\epsilon$. We propose a more efficient quantum strategy based on port-based teleportation, which stores the isometry channel in a program state using only $n = \Theta(1/\sqrt{\epsilon})$ queries, achieving a quadratic improvement over the classical strategy. As an application, we extend our approach to general quantum channels, achieving improved program cost compared to prior results by Gschwendtner, Bluhm, and Winter [Quantum \textbf{5}, 488 (2021)].

It has been revealed that arXiv:2105.06037v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum-enhanced metrology has achieved remarkable precision in parameter estimation, but extending these advantages to continuous time-dependent fields (waveform sensing) remains a formidable challenge due to the infinite-dimensional nature of the signal. Here, we report the first experimental realization of a room-temperature solid-state quantum oscilloscope based on a sequential quantum difference amplification strategy. Within a zero-order-hold reconstruction framework, our method completely bypasses the need for massive entanglement. Crucially, we demonstrate that the overall waveform reconstruction error unequivocally follows the theoretically predicted Heisenberg scaling of \(O(N^{-1/2})\), decisively surpassing the classical \(O(N^{-1/3})\) limit. This transformative precision requires approximately 30-fold fewer quantum resources than conventional methods to achieve the same waveform error. Furthermore, we demonstrate the reconstruction of a multicomponent waveform and distinctly resolve weak high-frequency components that are entirely drowned in the shot noise of classical sampling. These results transition quantum metrology from parameter estimation into a practical instrument, establishing a genuine quantum advantage in continuous waveform reconstruction and paving the way for critical applications such as nanoscale nuclear magnetic resonance imaging, where detecting extremely weak signals is crucial for resolving molecular structures.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.17110v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.

arXiv:2101.10821v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a theoretical protocol for reconstructing the density matrix of a single-electron spin qubit using spin-polarized transport. The system consists of a quantum dot coupled to ferromagnetic reservoirs and subject to a magnetic field lying in the $xy$ plane of the Bloch sphere. Spin-dependent tunneling events measured along the $x\pm$, $y\pm$, and $z\pm$ quantization axes give rise to probability distributions that encode the quantum state of the qubit. The open-system dynamics are described using a Lindblad master equation, which captures the time evolution of the spin under continuous coupling to the reservoirs. By counting tunneling events for four different magnetic alignments, we formulate a scheme for reconstructing the full density matrix of the qubit. The resulting simulation data are analyzed using Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) as a supervised machine-learning post-processing tool to reconstruct smooth time-dependent density-matrix elements from the measured probability distributions. The proposed model enables complete access to the open-system density matrix, including both population probabilities and relative phase information. Successful state reconstruction demonstrates the validity and robustness of the approach, highlighting its applicability to experimentally accessible spin-transport platforms.

This is the case of Differential Interference Contrast (DIC) microscopes. However, environmental disturbances such as acoustic vibrations, air currents, temperature shifts, and mechanical drifts cause random phase noise that degrades the precision attainable in the estimation of the unknown phase shift. Although there are tools to compensate for these random phase drifts, such using common path interference techniques or phase stabilization systems, these are not always an option and its introduction is generally at the expense of device simplicity and robustness. Here we introduce a quantum version of Differential Interference Contrast microscopy (qDIC), that makes use of quantum interference for polarization analysis. When compared with standard schemes that make use of coherent light, our approach shows that the transfer of classical DIC microscopy into the quantum domain offers a route towards quantum-enhanced resilience to environmental disturbances, allowing the enhancement of phase sensitivity without sacrificing the simplicity and robustness of the optical setup.

Our key insight is to model the response to small corrections around a policy proposal in an affine form that enables fast optimization. We refine a frozen imitation policy using an \textit{action-affine world model} (A\textsuperscript{2}WM), trained offline from perturbed policy rollouts. Conditioned on history and the proposal, the model directly predicts a nominal trajectory and a linear action response over the full horizon. With quadratic costs and linear constraints, refinement becomes a cheap quadratic program (QP), requiring only one model evaluation and one QP solve per control step. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to combine an action-affine world model with QP-based inference-time refinement of frozen imitation policies. Across four manipulation tasks, our framework achieves the highest success rate among evaluated baselines, adding only 4.2 ms of mean refinement latency per control step, excluding base-policy sampling.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.13370v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A humanoid that dances to streamed music must commit each motion chunk before it has heard the music that chunk accompanies, and must continue from motion it has already committed. We present AHEADance, a robot-native streaming dance generator executed on a humanoid robot by a whole-body tracker. ListenAhead conditions each chunk on heard music and a frozen music model's forecasts of the coming music, aligned to their target times and weighted by reliability. The forecasts carry the timing of upcoming beats almost as well as the actual future; with them, the generator is better synchronized with the music and concentrates more motion energy at its song's beat frequency. Commit Forcing trains continuation from the model's own committed chunks, updating both the latent history and the decoded boundary of the next chunk; it reduces low activity from 83.5% to 10.3%, the level of real dance. Three music evaluators, each validated on real G1 dance, test synchronization, song and style. On a physical Unitree G1, it dances while the music plays and comes to rest when it stops, without a fall. Project page: https://ihcr.github.io/AHEADance.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.22341v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For weak-phase objects, scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) with a far-field detector transfers at most half of the phase information per electron that Zernike phase-contrast (ZPC) conventional transmission electron microscopy (CTEM) achieves. We propose APEX (Apex Phase-plate EXit-wave imaging), a scanned-probe mode that combines a defocused probe, a $\pi/2$ phase element in a magnified image of the probe crossover, and in-focus image-plane detection at each scan position. It applies the generalized Zernike framework of Dwyer and Paganin to a scanned probe. In a linear model of a thin weak-phase object with an ideal phase dot, APEX transfers nearly the full Zernike Fisher information over a wide band, substantially more than diffraction-plane four-dimensional STEM (4D-STEM). In idealized simulations of myoglobin in vitreous ice at a cryo-EM dose (elastic scattering only, no chromatic aberration, full coherence), ideal-dot APEX at a probe defocus of 1 $\mu$m reconstructs the phase more accurately than defocused 4D-STEM ptychography with one untuned probe setting. At a defocus of about 25 $\mu$m, a crossed laser phase plate (XLPP) acts as the $\pi/2$ element, and APEX of a periodic specimen cell comes close to CTEM with the same plate. In two dimensions, this mode is equivalent to laser phase-plate CTEM of a small, scanned area. A single simulated APEX scan with the XLPP also separates two myoglobin phase screens 150 nm apart in vacuum, at known depths, which is not possible with one ZPC CTEM exposure.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (255 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.11148v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robots that travel long distances through public outdoor spaces must do more than avoid obstacles: they must remain on terrain suited to their mobility and decide when to proceed, yield, or detour around pedestrians, cyclists, vehicles, traffic signals, and temporary restrictions. These decisions are difficult because their correctness often depends on how a scene evolves, such as whether an approaching car is slowing or a cyclist will cross the robot's path. Vision-language models (VLMs) can interpret such cues, but they reason over images that lack metric geometry and motion. Supplying this evidence at every step is too slow for real-time navigation, and hand-crafted triggers cannot anticipate the open-ended variety of outdoor situations. We present MOSU2, a long-range navigation system with two-stage trajectory selection, in which first-stage contextual reasoning determines when additional evidence is needed and what to retrieve. Only when an interaction remains unresolved does the first stage trigger the second stage to retrieve geometric and dynamic information and align it with scene context to make navigation decisions. Building on MOSU, MOSU2 follows routes from GPS-based route planning and filters candidate trajectories through multi-modal traversability analysis before selecting a trajectory to move the robot. In real-world experiments spanning stop gestures, construction sites, crosswalks, and roads shared with vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians, MOSU2 raises mean navigation success from 61.8% to 94.2% and condition-detection accuracy from 72.2% to 91.4% over its single-image predecessor, at about 2.2 times its mean decision latency. Project website: https://jinggm.github.io/mosu2/.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (165 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.07621v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The protective separation zone of a collaborative robot cell is commonly dimensioned for a worst case that disregards where the operator is actually present during the task. This paper presents a camera-based, data-driven method that configures this zone from observed operator occupancy. Operator positions accumulated over several production shifts are aggregated into an occupancy heatmap, from which a protective field is derived that trades off the achievable robot velocity against the required safety distance, following the speed and separation monitoring principle of ISO/TS 15066. The resulting configuration is advisory, that is, reviewed within the risk assessment rather than applied autonomously to the robot controller. The method, which builds on a pose-based perception pipeline with activity recognition, was evaluated in two operational cells at two industrial partners, where the protective field could be reduced by approximately 17% and a productivity increase of 9% was measured. However, adoption proved to depend on more than the demonstrated gain alone.

VLALagBench: Understanding When and Why VLA Inference Latency Matters

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (199 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.03103v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward general-purpose robot manipulation. While inference latency can affect task success in a constantly evolving physical world, the relationship between latency and task success rate remains poorly understood. In this paper, we introduce VLALagBench, a comprehensive benchmark for studying VLA inference latency sensitivity across task types, object speeds, execution modes (synchronous and asynchronous), and VLA policies. Using VLALagBench, we find that even a modest inference latency of 100 ms can nearly halve task success on moving targets, with sensitivity varying substantially across tasks and policies. These differences reflect task-specific requirements for precision and continuous motion. By overlapping inference with action execution, asynchronous execution can recover some of the lost success at the cost of more frequent inference requests. Building on these findings, we develop an empirical model that predicts task success from limited calibration data, achieving root-mean-square prediction errors of only 5.7-7.8% across various VLA policies. Given an inference system's latency and per-robot throughput, these predictions guide the selection of system-specific VLA algorithm configurations to maximize task success. We believe VLALagBench and these findings provide a solid foundation for future robotics algorithm-system co-design.

Veloxity: Towards Memory-Safe UAV Embedded Firmware using the Rust Programming Language

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (171 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2610.41053v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent years have witnessed increased momentum towards memory-safe programming languages for safety-critical systems. Memory-safe languages can eliminate entire classes of common software errors that have historically required extensive analysis and expenditure to avoid. Nevertheless, memory-safe language adoption in aerospace remains fragmented and incomplete, particularly for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Recent Rust UAV projects either run only in simulation, are closed source, or have not been integrated with an established autonomy ecosystem and tested against existing C/C++ firmware. To address this gap, we present Veloxity: an open-source embedded UAV autopilot written in the memory-safe Rust programming language. Veloxity lowers the barrier to using memory-safe languages within modern ecosystems by providing a minimal, modular foundation for autonomous UAVs. We compare Veloxity to equivalent autopilots written in C++ in simulation, with hardware testbenches, and via outdoor waypoint-following flight tests, demonstrating functional parity with improved performance. These results indicate that modern memory-safe languages are a viable option for reliable and performant firmware for autonomous aerospace systems.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (166 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Complex mobility edges from competing localization channels in non-Hermitian quasicrystals

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (166 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22336v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Non-Hermitian localization transitions often accompany multiple mobility edges, but their physical origin can be ambiguous. To address the issue, we introduce an extension of the Ganeshan-Pixley-Das Sarma model with both asymmetric hopping and complex onsite potential, thereby incorporating a broad range of non-Hermitian quasiperiodic chains. Its solution reveals two energy-dependent localization contributions manifested as distinct Lyapunov growth scales, whose competition determines the structure of mobility edges. We derive exact Lyapunov exponents via Avila's global theory, obtain thresholds of the two channels on complex-energy plane, and formulate a selection rule that distinguishes physical mobility edges from suppressed analytical candidates. The channel that uniquely controls localization can switch with energy, producing complex mobility edges of non-Hermitian origins. Nonreciprocal hopping further shifts the thresholds and alters the bulk energy patterns. Numerical spectra and finite-size localization diagnostics confirm the theory. Our work thus provides a unified framework for characterizing phase transitions and mobility edges under competing localization mechanisms in non-Hermitian quasicrystals.

#21752. Actuator-Aware Observer Inputs for Cascade ADRC of Quadrotors Under Rotor Lag, Measurement Delay and Sensor Noise

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (245 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Actuator-Aware Observer Inputs for Cascade ADRC of Quadrotors Under Rotor Lag, Measurement Delay and Sensor Noise

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (245 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2610.39126v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In sampled cascade linear active disturbance rejection control (LADRC) of quadrotors, the extended-state observer is usually driven by the instantaneous command, although the delayed measurement reflects an earlier, rotor-filtered acceleration. This simulation and software-in-the-loop (SITL) study examines actuator-aware (AA) observer inputs: the altitude and attitude observers use the limited virtual input filtered by a rotor-lag model and aligned with the measurement delay, and the horizontal observers use the acceleration reconstructed from the measured attitude. Fixed gains are selected on the sampled model under sensitivity and step-response requirements and covariance-based ceilings on the noise-induced control increment, including the path from position noise to the inner loop. In 30 paired set-point trials, the two AA designs reach position root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 19.2 and 16.9~mm, versus 65.5~mm for a proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller tuned under the same requirements, with lower rotor-command increments. Ablations attribute the improvement to the rotor-lag model and the measured-attitude input; delay alignment is negligible at the nominal 5-ms delay. PX4 SITL runs reproduce these results within 2~mm. Behind the PX4 state estimator, the white-noise ceilings no longer describe the loop. After redesign with an identified estimation-error model, one AA design reduces the set-point RMSE from 59.1 to 44.0~mm with a 15\% lower quantized rotor-command increment, whereas the half-gain variant is worse than the PID. With fixed gains, the AA designs tolerate less unmodelled rotor lag and delay than the PID. Hardware validation remains future work.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Quantum Interband-Coherence-Driven Inverse Faraday Effect in Intrinsic Graphene

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (147 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22320v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The inverse Faraday effect converts the angular momentum of circularly polarized light into a quasistatic magnetization, providing a fundamental route to ultrafast optical control of magnetic fields. We develop an analytical quantum theory of this effect in intrinsic graphene, where massless Dirac fermions, electron-hole symmetry, and weak spin-orbit coupling suppress conventional population-based interpretations. We show that in intrinsic graphene, the helicity-dependent orbital magnetization arises from the off-diagonal zero-harmonic component of the second-order density matrix, rather than from intraband carrier circulation or diagonal population imbalance. We obtain closed expressions for the induced temporal surface magnetization, its finite-pulse dynamics, and the nonlocal stray magnetic field generated by the two-dimensional (2D) source. Optical helicity, frequency, pulse envelope, and beam profile independently control the response. Our results identify intrinsic graphene as an ideal platform for coherent orbital optomagnetism in 2D Dirac matter.
